kava.name: kava
kava.summary: A plant native to the Pacific Islands and the psychoactive ceremonial drink made from its root, producing relaxing effects without significant cognitive impairment.

earth-oven.name: Earth oven
earth-oven.summary: One of the oldest cooking methods, a heated pit in the ground used to bake, smoke or steam food, still used ceremonially in the Pacific today.

breadfruit.name: Breadfruit
breadfruit.summary: A tree species in the mulberry family whose fruit, tasting like bread when cooked, spread through Oceania via the Austronesian expansion and was bred in Polynesia.

cook-islands.name: Cook Islands
cook-islands.summary: A self-governing Polynesian island nation in the South Pacific, in free association with New Zealand, made up of 15 islands with its capital at Avarua on Rarotonga.

tapa-cloth.name: Tapa cloth
tapa-cloth.summary: A barkcloth made across the Pacific islands, especially Tonga, Samoa and Fiji; called kapa in Hawaii.

saudeleur-dynasty.name: Saudeleur dynasty
saudeleur-dynasty.summary: The first organized government to unite Pohnpei island, ruling from about 1100 to 1628 CE. Legend describes its rulers as foreign and increasingly oppressive, until they were overthrown by the invader Isokelekel.

pohnpei.name: Pohnpei
pohnpei.summary: The largest island of the Federated States of Micronesia, home to the megalithic ruined city of Nan Madol, begun in the 8th or 9th century.

nan-madol.name: Nan Madol
nan-madol.summary: A lagoon city of artificial islets linked by canals on Pohnpei, capital of the Saudeleur dynasty until about 1628, later nicknamed the 'Venice of the Pacific.'

tongatapu.name: Tongatapu
tongatapu.summary: The main island of Tonga and site of its capital, Nukuʻalofa, home to most of the country's population and its main center of trade.

aho-eitu.name: ʻAhoʻeitu
aho-eitu.summary: In Tongan oral tradition, the son of a god and a mortal woman who became the first king of the Tuʻi Tonga dynasty in the early 10th century.

tu-i-tonga.name: Tuʻi Tonga
tu-i-tonga.summary: A line of Tongan kings beginning in the 10th century with the mythical ʻAhoʻeitu, holding political power until yielding to the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua in the 15th century; the title itself ended in 1865.

tagaloa.name: Tagaloa
tagaloa.summary: The supreme god of Samoan mythology, regarded as creator of the universe and chief of all gods, whose worship predates Christianity and Islam in the islands.

kupe.name: Kupe
kupe.summary: Polynesian explorer credited in Māori history with being the first to discover New Zealand, around 1000–1300 CE, making him central to the origins of the Māori people.

kuram-r-tini.name: Kuramārōtini
kuram-r-tini.summary: Figure in Māori mythology, daughter of chief Toto, who sailed to New Zealand with the explorer Kupe after he tricked her husband Hoturapa overboard; said by some to have named the land Aotearoa.

hoturapa.name: Hoturapa
hoturapa.summary: In Māori tradition, a chief of Hawaiki whose wife owned the canoe Matahourua; tricked into diving overboard by his friend Kupe, who then sailed off with his wife.

te-wheke-a-muturangi.name: Te Wheke-a-Muturangi
te-wheke-a-muturangi.summary: A monstrous octopus in Māori mythology, a pet of the sorcerer Muturangi, said to have been destroyed by the navigator Kupe after a great battle.

hawaiki.name: Hawaiki
hawaiki.summary: In Polynesian folklore, the original homeland of the Polynesians before their dispersal across the Pacific, also featured as an underworld in Māori stories.

kumulipo.name: Kumulipo
kumulipo.summary: Hawaiian creation chant first recorded in the 18th century, including a genealogy of Hawaiian royalty, composed for Kalaninuiamamao and passed down to his daughter.

hahake-district.name: Hahake District
hahake-district.summary: One of the five districts of Wallis and Futuna in the Pacific Ocean, located on Wallis Island and part of the Chiefdom of Uvea.

k-kako.name: Kōkako
k-kako.summary: A forest bird native to New Zealand, slate-grey with wattles and a black mask, once called the New Zealand crow though unrelated to crows; one species is endangered, the other likely extinct.

makahiki.name: Makahiki
makahiki.summary: Ancient Hawaiian New Year festival honoring the god Lono, lasting four lunar months with feasting, rest, and a ban on labor and warfare.

lono.name: Lono
lono.summary: A Hawaiian god of fertility, agriculture, rain, music and peace, honored during the annual Makahiki festival.

tiki.name: Kiʻi
tiki.summary: The Hawaiian cognate of Tiki, the first man of Polynesian mythology; in Māori tradition Tiki was made by the gods and later found the first woman in a pond.

k-ne.name: Kāne
k-ne.summary: The highest of the three major Hawaiian deities, worshipped as the god of procreation, creator of life, and ancestor of chiefs and commoners, associated with dawn, sun and sky.

austronesian-peoples.name: Austronesian peoples
austronesian-peoples.summary: Peoples descended from a prehistoric seaborne migration out of Taiwan around 3000–1500 BCE, who used sails and outrigger boats to spread across the Indo-Pacific, from Madagascar to Easter Island and New Zealand.

mangaia.name: Mangaia
mangaia.summary: The southernmost and second-largest of the Cook Islands, once heavily populated but now much reduced after the decline of its pineapple industry.

marquesas-islands.name: Marquesas Islands
marquesas-islands.summary: Volcanic island group in French Polynesia, settled around the 10th century AD by voyagers from West Polynesia and named after a 16th-century Spanish viceroy of Peru.

outrigger-boat.name: Outrigger Canoe
outrigger-boat.summary: A watercraft with one or more lateral floats attached to the main hull, ranging from small canoes to large sailing vessels, which enabled the Austronesian expansion across the ocean.

tui-manu-a.name: Tui Manuʻa
tui-manu-a.summary: Title held by the ruler or paramount chief of the Manuʻa Islands, whose realm grew into a wide-reaching Polynesian network sometimes called the Samoan Empire.

manu-a-islands.name: Manuʻa Islands
manu-a-islands.summary: A group of Samoan islands, now part of American Samoa, that served as the political centre of the Tui Manuʻa Empire for many centuries.

mu-a-tongatapu.name: Mu'a
mu-a-tongatapu.summary: A small town on Tongatapu, in the Kingdom of Tonga, that was for centuries the capital of the Tu'i Tonga Empire, known for its ancient royal burial tombs.

tabua.name: Tabua
tabua.summary: A polished sperm whale tooth central to Fijian culture, traditionally given as a gift in negotiations, weddings and funerals.

kapu-hawaiian-culture.name: Kapu
kapu-hawaiian-culture.summary: The ancient Hawaiian code of laws governing lifestyle, gender roles, politics, and religion, in which breaking a rule was often punished by death; related to the Polynesian concept of taboo.

tapu-polynesian-culture.name: Tapu
tapu-polynesian-culture.summary: A Polynesian concept of something holy or sacred involving rules and prohibitions; the source of the English word "taboo", from Captain Cook's 1777 visit to Tonga.

k.name: Kū
k.summary: One of the four great gods of Hawaiian religion, worshiped under many names including Kūkāʻilimoku, whose rites uniquely included human sacrifice.

kanaloa.name: Kanaloa
kanaloa.summary: A Hawaiian god symbolized by the squid or octopus, associated with the ocean and seamanship, and traditionally paired with the god Kāne.

taputapuatea-marae.name: Taputapuatea marae
taputapuatea-marae.summary: A large marae complex at Opoa on Raiatea, once considered the central temple and religious center of Eastern Polynesia; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017.

ra-i-tea.name: Ra'iātea
ra-i-tea.summary: The second-largest of the Society Islands in French Polynesia, regarded as the ancient centre of eastern Polynesia and likely starting point of migrations to Hawaii and other Pacific islands.
